newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Deng death glances off southern "hearts of stone".
newsitem.headline: Deng death glances off southern "hearts of stone".

text.p: China's booming south barely blinked on Thursday at the death of Deng Xiaoping, the pioneer and architect of the region's economic revolution.
The whirl and frenzy of economic activity that is transforming the Pearl River Basin into a copy of Hong Kong continued regardless and few seemed to believe Deng's death would affect their future.
"Most Chinese people are not paying much attention to this and don't have much of an opinion about this," restaurant manager Chan Guizhi told visitors to the city of Dongguan.
"Most people when they heard the news this morning didn't know what to make of it."
Local radio began carrying Beijing's announcement of Deng's death at about 9 a.m (0100 GMT) and repeated it on the hour.
Chen, a taxi driver in Shenzhen, just over the border from Hong Kong, said city streets were normal.

"Except for one thing, passengers were very busy at their mobile phones discussing markets," he said. "When I heard on the radio of Deng's death, I almost jumped out of my seat worrying about my stocks."
Chen said he invested about 3,000 yuan ($385) in shares shortly after arriving in the boomtown a year ago.
"Because people in Shenzhen came from all over the country seaching for good life, most of them have hearts of stone," the taxi driver said. He declined to give his full name.
The casual response to Deng's death was a great contrast to passing of Chairman Mao Zedong in 1976, when the country ground to a halt to mourn.
Despite the general indifference, Li Tongnuo, a Dongguan security guard said Deng's death had a great impact on her.
"I feel extremely sad, extremely sad," she said. "He brought great comfort to the people. He brought them happiness and an easier life."
Tailor Wen Jingsen felt much the same. He told visitors he felt "great regret" at Deng's passing but that not much would change.
"It will not affect China's future. Deng Xiaoping has been retired for several years already. China's policies have already been arranged," he said.
"He opened up our country and promoted our economic development. That is a great contribution."
Xu, an electrical engineer working in the border town of Shenzhen, echoed similar sentiments.

"I will miss Deng because I wouldn't be in Shenzhen if it was not for him," said Xu, who migrated from a village in the same province four years earlier. "I am earning about four times as much as I used to."
